title: Milestone: Inside the Mind
objective: After this level you can connect perception, learning, memory, motivation and emotion into one picture of how experience becomes action.
summary: An emotion combines a judgment, a body state, an expression and a feeling. Put Chapter 5 together, and experience turns into action through appraisal, arousal and motivation.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Follow one moment from feeling to action.
cards.body: Your teacher asks you to give a talk to the class. In a moment your mind judges the situation, your body reacts, a feeling arrives, and you want to do something about it. Two students can get the same request and feel completely different. This chapter gave you the pieces; here they are in one chain.

cards.headline: Four parts of one emotion
cards.body: Psychologists describe an emotion as four things at once: what you feel inside, how you show it, how you appraise the situation, and how your body responds. In appraisal theory, that judgment comes first and steers the feeling. One student sees a chance to shine and feels happy; another dreads public speaking and feels uneasy. Same event, different judgment, different emotion.

items.label: Before the feeling
points: Your judgment of the event shapes what you feel
Two people can feel differently about the same event

items.label: The feeling
points: Two-factor view: arousal plus a label from the situation
Intense and about something, unlike a longer, milder mood

items.label: After the feeling
points: Drives push to restore balance; incentives pull
What ends a drive tends to become a habit

cards.headline: Milestone: inside the mind
learned: How a judgment, a body state and a label combine into an emotion that can move you to act.
Why drives push, incentives pull, and an expected reward can take the fun out of an activity.
Why ego depletion and the pen-in-mouth smile shrank when many labs retested them.
What counting dreams and testing tired minds showed that people's own impressions missed.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap: why can two students feel differently about the same request to give a talk?

options.label: Only one of them has a body that reacts
Emotions come before any judgment is made
options.rationale: In appraisal theory, the judgment comes first.

options.label: They judge the moment differently, and that shapes the feeling
Moods and emotions are exactly the same thing
options.rationale: Moods are longer and milder than emotions.

questions.explanation: In appraisal theory, your judgment of an event comes first and shapes the emotion, so the same request can bring happiness or unease.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap, from Level 42: who first drew Maslow's hierarchy as a pyramid?

options.label: Abraham Maslow, in 1943
Louis Tay and Ed Diener, in 2011
options.rationale: They tested the needs across 123 countries.

options.label: Todd Bridgman, in 2019
options.rationale: Bridgman traced the pyramid; he didn't draw it.

options.label: Charles McDermid, in 1960

questions.explanation: A 2019 history traced the pyramid to consulting psychologist Charles McDermid's 1960 article; Maslow never drew one.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap, from Level 44: what did the 2016 test of ego depletion in 23 labs find?

options.label: An effect near zero
A much larger effect than in 1998
An effect only in people who ate radishes twice
That willpower recharges after exactly an hour
options.rationale: The study made no such claim.

questions.explanation: The 2016 multi-lab replication, with 2,141 people in 23 labs, found an ego-depletion effect near zero.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap, from Level 47: what did the 2022 Many Smiles study find about deliberately posed smiles?

options.label: They made people feel sadder
They raised feelings of happiness
They had no effect in any country
They worked only with a pen in the mouth
options.rationale: The pen method was the least conclusive.

questions.explanation: Copying smiling faces or deliberately posing a smile raised happiness; the pen method was less conclusive.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap, from Level 48: after 14 days of short sleep, how did volunteers judge their own sleepiness?

options.label: They rated it only a little higher despite growing deficits
They felt exhausted and stopped taking the tests
options.rationale: They kept testing; their ratings stayed low.

options.label: They felt sharper than before the study
They rated it accurately, matching their scores

questions.explanation: In Van Dongen's study, sleepiness ratings barely rose after the first days while thinking deficits kept building.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap, from Level 49: what did counting 635 lab dream reports show about the typical dream?

options.label: A bizarre scene with no link to real life
A coded message about hidden childhood urges
options.rationale: That was Freud's view, not the counting result.

options.label: A clear, realistic story about ordinary things
A dream with no other people in it

questions.explanation: The typical dream was a clear, coherent story of a realistic situation with the dreamer and other people doing ordinary things.

questions.prompt: Inside the Mind recap: the chain says a feeling depends on how you read the moment. Which Level 45 study showed arousal taking its label from the situation?

options.label: Schachter and Singer's epinephrine study
Baumeister's radish study
options.rationale: That tested willpower, not emotion labels.

options.label: Strack's pen-in-mouth study
Lepper's magic marker study

questions.explanation: Men with unexplained epinephrine arousal were likelier to feel euphoria or anger matching the actor: the situation supplied the label.
